strengths: Novel problem formulation: this appears to be the first generative model producing large-scale 3D semantic urban scene layouts directly as 3D primitives (rather than voxel grids or 2.5D layouts), which is a meaningful new direction for controllable scene synthesis.

Well-motivated hybrid representation: rasterized ground maps plus vectorized cuboid/ellipsoid primitives, with a disentangled joint latent space (z_G, z_O) that cleanly enables ground-conditioned object generation, inpainting, and outpainting without fine-tuning (RePaint-style latent manipulation). The latent-split ablation (AP3D 62.11 vs 53.78 when decoders share the latent) supports the design choice.

The Cholesky-based joint encoding of orientation and size is a technically sound contribution; the derivation in the supplementary shows sign-flip invariance and unique decomposition, and the synthetic-data ablation against quaternion encoding (Fig. 4b) provides concrete evidence of improved numerical stability across training sizes.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: reconstruction comparisons against SemCity at multiple resolutions with careful accounting of query-point subsampling, generation metrics (Prec./Rec./FID/IS) across DiT-B/L/XL, and three ablations of the LVAE design.

Honest and thorough treatment of limitations: the authors discuss the precision/recall metric sensitivity, provide a dedicated analysis (Fig. 9) of how sampling strategy and neighborhood size affect the metrics, and include explicit failure cases (Fig. 10). The supplementary is detailed enough to support reproducibility (architecture sizes, loss weights, training schedules, dataset split procedure).
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (KITTI-360) and essentially a single baseline (SemCity), which was retrained by the authors on their voxelized data. Given the scarcity of annotated data this is understandable, but it makes it hard to assess generality of the approach.

The generation evaluation is done on 2D rendered semantic maps (top-down orthographic projections) with FID/Precision/Recall/IS, not with any 3D-aware metric. The absolute Precision/Recall values are extremely low for SemCity (0.0288/0.0472), and the authors themselves note these metrics are highly sensitive to the real-sample sampling protocol — they introduced a custom distance-thresholded sampling strategy. This raises the question of whether the protocol disproportionately disadvantages the voxel baseline, and no comparison to prior published numbers is possible.

Downstream applications (inpainting, outpainting, object-level editing, street-view synthesis) are demonstrated only qualitatively; there is no quantitative evaluation of editing fidelity, consistency, or usefulness, which weakens the 'controllable and editable' claims in the title.

The reconstruction comparison has a representational asymmetry: primitive scenes are voxelized only for evaluation, so the IoU comparison partially measures the representation rather than the generative model; the memory-efficiency claim (2.52 MB vs 8 MB) is largely a property of the chosen representation.

Fixed-size set prediction with a dataset-determined query count (N=514, per-category 95th percentile) means scenes exceeding these counts are truncated at the data-processing stage, limiting scalability to denser scenes; the approach is tightly tailored to KITTI-360 statistics.

Geometric fidelity is inherently limited by coarse primitives and rasterized ground extrusion, and the authors acknowledge issues such as floating/disconnected small objects; no mechanism is evaluated for finer-grained structure.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper makes a credible case that voxel-based representations are a bottleneck for large-scale 3D semantic scene generation, and the proposed hybrid representation (rasterized ground + vectorized object primitives) is a sensible and, to the authors' credit, apparently unexplored formulation for outdoor scenes.

The Cholesky-based parameterization of joint orientation/scale (supplementary Sec. B.1) is technically sound, with a correct proof of sign-invariance, symmetry, and positive-definiteness, and it is empirically validated against quaternion encoding on controlled synthetic data across training sizes (Fig. 4b).

The experimental section is more thorough than typical: reconstruction comparison at multiple resolutions, ablations of latent split, joint vs. separate training, and object parameterization; the supplementary provides substantial architectural, loss-weighting, and dataset-split detail that supports reproducibility.

The authors are candid about limitations (Sec. 5 and supplementary Sec. E), including coarse geometric fidelity, static scenes, and outpainting failure cases, and they show actual failure examples (Fig. 10).
Downstream applications (inpainting, outpainting, ground-conditioned object generation) require no fine-tuning, which is an attractive practical property stemming from the disentangled latent design.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is narrow: all experiments are on a single dataset (KITTI-360), and the only quantitative baseline is SemCity [29], retrained by the authors with a modified query-point configuration (400K instead of default 40K). The headline claim of '3x memory reduction with comparable quality' depends heavily on this re-tuned baseline; at the configuration most favorable to SemCity it achieves mIoU 93.81 vs. 70.27 for PrITTI, a substantial reconstruction gap that is framed as a 'trade-off' but arguably undercuts the representation-quality claim.

The generation comparison (Table 1) is computed on 2D top-down orthographic semantic projections using FID/IS/Precision/Recall. These metrics are indirect proxies for 3D layout quality and, as the authors themselves document at length (supplementary Fig. 9), are highly sensitive to sampling strategy and neighborhood size. There is no 3D distributional metric, no user study, and no evaluation of physical plausibility (e.g., object-ground consistency, collision rates) that would substantiate 'more realistic layouts' beyond visual impression.

All downstream applications (inpainting, outpainting, object editing, street-view synthesis) are evaluated only qualitatively. There are no quantitative measures of edit locality, boundary consistency, or content preservation for inpainting/outpainting, so the central 'controllability and editability' claim rests largely on selected visual examples.

The core representation is quite coarse: fixed-size set prediction (N=514 queries, counts truncated at the 95th percentile per category), cuboid/ellipsoid primitives, and 2D-extruded ground surfaces. The paper concedes this loses fine structures (fences, pole-mounted fixtures), but the practical consequence is that the 'compact and controllable' representation trades away exactly the geometric richness that motivates 3D scene generation for simulation.

Controllability is thin in practice: the only conditioning signal demonstrated is a discretized vegetation-density label derived from dataset percentiles (supplementary Sec. A). Calling this 'controllable generation' as a first-class contribution overstates what is shown.

Technical novelty is incremental. The pipeline is a standard two-stage LDM (VGG-style VAE encoder + DiT + RePaint-style resampling), applied to a new data representation. The Cholesky encoding is elegant but closely related to existing symmetric-positive-definite / 6D rotation parameterizations, and its empirical advantage is demonstrated only on a synthetic single-vehicle task.
Photo-realistic street-view synthesis (Fig. 1, Sec. 4.3) relies entirely on a pre-trained Urban Architect ControlNet; this application adds little and should not count toward the contribution.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code or data release is mentioned anywhere in the manuscript, and the custom train/test split, class merging, and loss weighting involve many undocumented-in-main-paper decisions.

Clarity issues: the reconstruction table (Fig. 3a) mixes trained-at-resolution and upsampled configurations in a way that is hard to parse, and the narrative around SemCity's mIoU 93.81 result is diffuse; the reader must reconstruct the fair comparison themselves.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper is the first to use vectorized 3D primitives as the fundamental generative unit for large-scale outdoor semantic scene synthesis, and the hybrid representation (rasterized ground + vectorized object primitives) is a sensible design that addresses genuine limitations of voxel grids (memory, fixed resolution, editability).

Strong empirical results against a reasonable baseline: PrITTI substantially outperforms SemCity on generative metrics (FID 51.3 vs 156.2, precision 0.45 vs 0.03) while using ~3x less per-scene memory (2.52 MB vs 8.00 MB), and the reconstruction comparison is conducted carefully — the authors retrained SemCity on their voxelized primitive data and analyzed the query-count/memory trade-off rather than cherry-picking a weak configuration.

Technically sound and well-motivated Cholesky-based parameterization: the derivation of the scatter-matrix encoding (sign-invariance, symmetry, positive-definiteness, unique decomposition) is clean, and the supporting ablation across training sizes shows a consistent advantage over quaternion encodings.

Comprehensive ablations of the LVAE design (latent split, joint vs. separate training), and the downstream applications (inpainting, outpainting, ground-conditioned object generation, primitive-level editing) follow naturally from the disentangled latent design without extra fine-tuning.

Above-average clarity and reproducibility: the supplementary material is unusually complete (loss formulations with exact weights, architectures, training schedules, dataset split construction, license information, and even failure cases), which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited: all experiments are on a single dataset (KITTI-360) and the generative comparison relies on a single baseline (SemCity). Other relevant baselines or representation choices (e.g., 2.5D map-based methods such as CityDreamer/Gaudigen adapted to this setting, or hierarchical voxel methods like XCube) are not compared, making it hard to judge whether the gains stem from the primitive representation specifically or from the stronger DiT backbone.

The generative metrics are non-standard and acknowledged by the authors themselves to be highly sensitive: precision/recall are computed on rendered 2D semantic maps with a custom distance-thresholded sampling protocol for reference frames, and FID/IS on semantic map renderings are unusual proxies for 3D layout quality. Although the sensitivity analysis in Fig. 9 is commendable, the reported headline numbers depend on these protocol choices.

The reconstruction comparison mixes representations: PrITTI is evaluated after voxelizing primitives for IoU/mIoU, which inherently smooths geometry, while SemCity is evaluated on its native voxel output. The comparison is still informative but not a like-for-like measure of representational fidelity.
The Cholesky vs. quaternion ablation is conducted on a synthetic single-object dataset rather than real scenes, so the claimed stability benefit is only indirectly validated on the actual task.

The fixed-size set prediction (per-category query counts at the 95th percentile) discards ground-truth instances during preprocessing, which may bias results and limits scalability to scenes exceeding the preset counts; the paper does not quantify the impact of discarded objects.

Controllability and editing applications (Figs. 1, 6, 12) are demonstrated qualitatively without quantitative validation (e.g., no user study or measure of edit consistency/realism), and the scene-level conditioning is limited to a single vegetation-density label.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel primitive-based paradigm for 3D semantic urban scene generation: a hybrid representation combining vectorized object primitives (cuboids/ellipsoids with a novel Cholesky-based 6D orientation+size encoding) and rasterized ground surfaces. This is a genuinely new direction for scene-level generation, distinct from prior voxel-based (SemCity, PDD, XCube) and 2.5D layout methods.

Strong quantitative evidence for the core claims: substantially better generative metrics than voxel baselines (FID 73.9 vs. 94.8 for the best baseline XCube; precision 0.712 vs 0.482; recall 0.491 vs 0.230), fastest inference (0.58 s), and constant low memory per scene (2.52 MB) with competitive reconstruction quality. The scaling results (DiT-B/L/XL) add credibility to the claim that primitives unlock diffusion transformer capabilities.

Comprehensive and thoughtful experiments: reconstruction metrics in both voxelized and primitive space (AP3D), ablations for the disentangled latent split (AP3D 62.12 -> 53.78 without it), joint vs. separate training, and a Cholesky vs. quaternion comparison. The precision/recall sensitivity analysis (Fig. 10, Sec. F) examining sample counts, sampling strategy, and neighborhood size k is unusually careful and improves trust in the evaluation.

Multiple downstream applications demonstrated without fine-tuning (inpainting, outpainting via a sliding-window latent manipulation, ground-conditioned object generation, instance-level editing, street-view synthesis), with extensive qualitative results in the supplementary.

The supplementary is thorough and honest: custom non-overlapping train/test split construction, full loss formulations, failure cases (Fig. 11), baseline training configurations (Tab. 7), and an explicit limitations section covering static scenes, fixed category set, raster resolution limits, and outpainting failure modes.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (KITTI-360) with a custom train/test split. Generalization to other urban environments, indoor scenes, or other primitive-annotated datasets is not demonstrated, and the custom split complicates comparison with prior published numbers.

Baseline fairness is imperfect. Primitives are voxelized for comparison, which the authors acknowledge disadvantages voxel-native methods' metrics, and PrITTI is evaluated with label-balanced conditional sampling while all baselines are unconditional; the paper itself notes precision/recall are highly sensitive to reference diversity. This weakens the head-to-head generative comparison, though the qualitative gap appears consistent.

The Cholesky vs. quaternion ablation (Fig. 4) is conducted only on a synthetic single-primitive task with random yaw, providing limited evidence for the claimed stability benefit in the full scene-level setting; no in-situ ablation on the real pipeline is reported.

The representation yields coarse geometry by design (cuboids/ellipsoids, rasterized ground); fine-grained structures (fences, pole-mounted attachments) reconstruct poorly, as shown in the failure cases. The paper is candid about this, but it limits geometric fidelity and usefulness for some simulation applications.

FID/IS are computed on 2D top-down semantic maps using an Inception backbone, which is not obviously well-calibrated for semantic map statistics; this is inherited from prior work but the metric's meaningfulness deserves more scrutiny given the margins reported.

Photo-realistic street-view synthesis is presented as a downstream application but relies on an off-the-shelf ControlNet from Urban Architect [45]; it is a demonstration rather than a contribution and shows some artifacts.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: while primitives are widely used for shape abstraction and parsing, using instance-level parameterized primitives as the generation target for large-scale 3D semantic urban scenes is novel, and the claim of being 'the first' appears well supported by the related work discussion.

The technical design is coherent and well-motivated: the hybrid representation (rasterized ground + vectorized primitives) is a sensible engineering choice given the difficulty of uniformly parameterizing polygonal ground surfaces, and the disentangled ground/object latent split directly enables downstream capabilities (ground-conditioned object inpainting) without additional training.

The Cholesky-based parameterization of object orientation and size is a clean solution to a real problem (quaternion sign ambiguity), and the supplementary provides a complete derivation; the ablation in Fig. 4 shows clear stability gains.

The experimental section is thorough for a first-of-its-kind system: reconstruction comparisons (Tab. 1), generation metrics (Tab. 3), DiT scaling results (DiT-B/L/XL), LVAE ablations (Tab. 2), sensitivity analysis of precision/recall under multiple sampling protocols (Fig. 10), and honest presentation of failure cases (Fig. 11) and baseline low-quality examples (Fig. 9).

The manuscript is generally well written, the two-stage pipeline is clearly described, and the supplementary contains sufficient implementation detail (losses, weights, schedules, dataset split construction) to support reproducibility, with code and models promised as publicly available.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a material concern. In Tab. 3, PrITTI is evaluated conditionally (balanced vegetation-density labels) while all baselines are unconditional. The authors argue the setup is fair, but conditioning on a label that correlates strongly with the dominant content (vegetation volume) plausibly reduces mode collapse and inflates precision/recall/FID relative to unconditional generation. A conditional comparison at matched protocol (e.g., unconditional PrITTI) is missing from the main table.

The generative evaluation protocol itself is acknowledged to be fragile: the authors state that precision/recall are 'highly sensitive' to sample size, reference diversity, and neighborhood size k, and the chosen configuration (1K maximally spaced references, k=3) was selected by the authors. Given this acknowledged sensitivity, the very large margins over baselines (e.g., FID 73.9 vs 94.8 for the next best) should be interpreted cautiously, and the headline claim of 'state-of-the-art generation quality' rests on a partially self-chosen protocol.

Metrics are computed by rendering scenes into 2D BEV semantic maps, a domain that structurally favors the proposed representation: crisp primitive outlines in BEV will produce different feature statistics than voxel-native outputs. Similarly, the reconstruction evaluation (Tab. 1) voxelizes the primitive representation, which the authors concede disadvantages PrITTI, yet the resulting lower IoU (90.58 vs 99.97 for XCube) makes the 'similar reconstruction quality' conclusion in the conclusion section somewhat overstated.

The Cholesky-vs-quaternion ablation (Fig. 4) is conducted only on synthetic single-object data (one zero-centered vehicle with random yaw), which is far from the multi-object, multi-category distribution of real scenes; the claimed numerical-stability benefit is therefore only weakly evidenced for the actual setting.

All experiments are on a single dataset (KITTI-360) with a custom train/test split and a custom label taxonomy, so generality across datasets, sensor conditions, or geography is untested; generalization claims in the abstract ('unlock the full capabilities of diffusion transformers') go beyond what a single-dataset study supports.

The representation itself is coarse: objects are cuboids/ellipsoids and ground is 2.5D extrusion, so fine-grained attachments, overhangs, and dense small structures are poorly captured (as shown in Fig. 11a). This limits usefulness for applications requiring geometric fidelity, and the paper largely relegates this to limitations rather than quantifying the geometric gap against real scene geometry.

Some claims of practical advantage over voxels (e.g., editability, memory scaling) are argued qualitatively or shown only on representative examples (Figs. 1, 6, 26) rather than measured; a quantitative user study or edit-consistency metric would substantially strengthen these claims.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: PrITTI is presented as the first primitive-based framework for large-scale 3D semantic urban scene generation, addressing real limitations of voxel-based representations (memory scaling, fixed resolution, poor editability).

Thoughtful technical design: the hybrid representation (rasterized ground + parameterized object primitives), the disentangled ground/object latent structure, and the DETR-style fixed-size set decoder are clearly described and well integrated with established components (VAE, DiT, RePaint-style latent manipulation).

The Cholesky-based parameterization of object orientation and size is a clean solution to quaternion/eigenvector sign ambiguity, and it is supported by a dedicated controlled ablation (Fig. 4, supplementary Sec. C) rather than asserted.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: comparisons against three recent voxel baselines (SemCity, PDD, XCube) at matched settings, ablations on latent split and joint vs. separate training, sensitivity analysis of precision/recall metrics, generation-time comparison, and an extensive supplementary with both good and failure examples for all methods.

Strong practical outcomes: competitive reconstruction with lower memory, substantially better generative metrics (FID, Precision/Recall, IS) and faster inference than all baselines, plus demonstrated downstream tasks (inpainting, outpainting, ground-conditioned object generation, object-level editing, street-view synthesis) enabled without fine-tuning.

Careful dataset handling: a custom non-overlapping train/test split of KITTI-360, transparent reporting of baselines' evaluation issues (e.g., SemCity-1M), and honest failure-case discussion (Fig. 11, supplementary Sec. G).
Clarity and reproducibility: the method, losses, architectures, training schedules, and category mappings are documented in detail, and code/models are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (KITTI-360). Given the claim of a general framework, a second domain (even an indoor or synthetic layout dataset) would substantially strengthen the generality claim.

The generative comparison has an asymmetry: PrITTI is evaluated class-conditionally (vegetation density) while all baselines are unconditional. The authors argue this is for label balancing, but conditional generation can inflate fidelity/diversity metrics; an unconditional PrITTI variant or additional conditioning for baselines would make the comparison cleaner.

The adapted evaluation protocol (rendering to BEV semantic maps for FID/Precision/Recall) is a custom construction; some metric choices (1K reference samples, neighborhood size k=3) are selected by the authors, and while sensitivity is analyzed, absolute FID values are not directly comparable to prior literature.

The representation trades geometric fidelity for compactness: reconstruction IoU/mIoU does not surpass the best voxel baselines (e.g., SemCity-1M mIoU 93.81 vs. 70.27), and known limitations (floating objects, coarse primitives, resolution-limited ground extrusion) are acknowledged. The editability advantage is shown qualitatively but not quantified (e.g., no user study or edit-consistency metric).

Controllability is currently limited to a single derived vegetation-density label; the framework's broader controllability claims rest on the architecture rather than demonstrated conditioning signals.
Duplicate/inflated reference entries in the bibliography (e.g., [39]/[40], [51]/[52]) and the incomplete URL in the abstract are presentation flaws that should be corrected.
